title: Why There Are So Many Bad Managers
author: Ethan Evans
summary: Ethan Evans argues that the prevalence of poor management is not explained by lack of intelligence or effort but by a structural failure: organizations promote their best individual contributors into management without giving them the training, coaching, or developmental runway that would allow them to become competent at the fundamentally different craft of leading people. The argument is built on an analogy: we would never put someone in an engineering role and expect them to figure out coding through trial and error, yet we do exactly that with management every day. Evans defines leadership as a craft — something that requires repetition, feedback, observation, reflection, and the hard experience of real situations over time — not a set of principles that can be absorbed in a training. He traces the failure pattern: the top performer gets promoted, defaults to doing the work themselves (because that is what made them successful), fails to develop or delegate, and becomes the kind of manager who is both overworked and underperforming as a leader. The article closes with what organizations, managers, and individual contributors can each do to address the problem.
points: The management promotion problem is structural, not personal: organizations reward individual contribution with a management title, then provide no development path for the entirely different skill set that management requires.

Leadership is a craft that must be developed through practice, coaching, and repeated experience with real situations — it cannot be downloaded through a seminar or a book, any more than coding can be learned by reading about it.

The promoted top performer's default — doing the work themselves rather than enabling others to do it — is not laziness or arrogance but the application of the only success strategy they know to a role where that strategy fails.

The 'you learn by doing' argument for management development has a specific shape: you learn to have difficult conversations by having them (with coaching and reflection), not by reading about them — which means organizations must create supported practice opportunities.

The gap between the skills that get someone promoted and the skills that would make them a good manager is not a bug in organizational systems; it reflects a genuine confusion about what management is and why it matters.

The reason so many managers struggle is not that they lack intelligence or effort. It’s that management is a craft that must be honed over many years, but we treat it like a promotion that occurs overnight.

The skills that made them successful in their previous role are no longer the skills that determine their success going forward. Yet in many organizations, there is little or no formal preparation for this transition.

There are certainly pieces of it that can be learned “academically” — frameworks, research studies, and principles that can help. But the actual practice of leadership is learned through repetition, coaching, observation, reflection, and feedback.
These are not skills most people magically acquire because they were good at their previous job and got promoted. So, the result is that many people become bad managers when they get that promotion.

The reason is usually the irrational fear that if they invest in training, people might leave and take that training with them to another company. Or that if they help people grow, they will ask for promotions or raises.

The Catch-22 One statistic captures the problem perfectly: Roughly 70% of people who leave a job do so because of some form of conflict or dissatisfaction with their manager. Many organizations are basically creating this scenario for themselves.
